steps.lessonTitle: Pick your training route
steps.title: Create your evidence folder
steps.where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
steps.action: On the physical host, open File Explorer and create a SONIC-Lab folder with subfolders Installers, Screenshots, Baselines, and Backups. Keep passwords elsewhere.
steps.expected: The four folders exist on storage with sufficient free space.

steps.lessonTitle: Pick your training route
steps.title: Record the version journey
steps.where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
steps.action: Create a lab note: VMware Workstation Pro on the host; Windows Server 2019 Desktop Experience on premises; Server 2019 Azure destination; migrate test workload/data; then upgrade that Azure member server to Server 2022.
steps.expected: Your note distinguishes moving an application from moving a whole VM.

steps.lessonTitle: Pick your training route
steps.title: Choose the required route
steps.where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
steps.action: Complete the Windows/AD core, SQL core, Azure foundations, and migration core in sidebar order. Leave MECM and high availability extensions until their setup checks pass.
steps.expected: DC01/DC02 and APP01 are prepared before the migration work.

steps.lessonTitle: Understand the map
steps.title: Know what each practice server does
steps.where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
steps.action: Open your lab notes on the Windows host. Write DC01 and DC02: manage practice users, sign-in and DNS. Write APP01: hosts the IIS test website and, in the separate help desk class, osTicket. Write SQL01: stores a practice database; it is not a website. Write DEST-DC01: owns the separate migrate.lab.example.test destination domain. Draw each server on VMnet2, then add the matching addresses from the earlier plan. For the DMZ class later, the new private IIS server moves to its own application network and only the gateway sits in the DMZ.
steps.expected: Your notes show each server name, its job, network and address. You can point to the website server without confusing it with a domain controller.

steps.lessonTitle: Prepare your laptop and downloads
steps.title: Confirm Workstation Pro
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: On your physical Windows PC, open VMware Workstation Pro > Help > About. Record the installed version. This course uses Workstation, not vCenter or ESXi.
steps.expected: The product is Workstation Pro and it can create Windows Server 2019 guests.

steps.lessonTitle: Prepare your laptop and downloads
steps.title: Obtain Server 2019 media
steps.where: Your Windows host · web browser for Microsoft Evaluation Center
steps.action: Use the Windows Server 2019 ISO your course or license administrator supplies. For local-only evaluation, open https://www.microsoft.com/evalcenter/evaluate-windows-server-2019 and download the 64-bit ISO. Save it under Installers.
steps.expected: The media is Windows Server 2019, not 2025.

steps.lessonTitle: Prepare your laptop and downloads
steps.title: Choose the media and license path
steps.where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
steps.action: Record language, edition, evaluation/licensed status, and whether Desktop Experience is available. The Azure upgrade exercise uses a licensed/pay-as-you-go 2019 Marketplace member VM with a matching 2022 upgrade path.
steps.expected: Your source and destination license choices are written down.

steps.lessonTitle: Prepare your laptop and downloads
steps.title: Check host resources
steps.action: On the host press Ctrl+Shift+Esc > Performance. Record available RAM and disk space. Start a tiny DC at 1 vCPU and 2048 MB RAM; keep a 60 GB growable system disk. A basic IIS test can start at 2 GB RAM; the full help desk uses 4 GB or more. SQL and MECM use their separate requirements. Shut down optional VMs you are not using; leave memory for your Windows host.
steps.expected: The host has enough free resources for the next required pair of VMs.

steps.lessonTitle: Build the isolated VMnet2 network
steps.title: Open Virtual Network Editor
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: On Windows 10 open VMware Workstation Pro. Choose Edit > Virtual Network Editor. Select Change Settings if shown and approve your administrator prompt.
steps.expected: The editor lets you change virtual networks.

steps.lessonTitle: Build the isolated VMnet2 network
steps.title: Create VMnet2 as Host-only
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: Select Add Network, choose VMnet2 and confirm. Select VMnet2 in the list, then select Host-only. Keep Connect a host virtual adapter to this network checked. Do not select NAT or Bridged.
steps.expected: VMnet2 is listed as Host-only. It has no NAT gateway or connection to your physical LAN.

steps.lessonTitle: Build the isolated VMnet2 network
steps.title: Set the private address range
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: With VMnet2 selected, enter Subnet IP 10.50.0.0 and Subnet mask 255.255.255.0. This /24 is the shared address range for DC01 and DC02.
steps.expected: The editor displays 10.50.0.0 and 255.255.255.0 for VMnet2.

steps.lessonTitle: Build the isolated VMnet2 network
steps.title: Turn off VMware DHCP
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: Clear Use local DHCP service to distribute IP addresses to VMs. We will type fixed addresses into the servers ourselves. Select Apply, then OK.
steps.expected: VMnet2 is saved as Host-only with DHCP off. There is no default gateway to record for this isolated network.

steps.lessonTitle: Build the isolated VMnet2 network
steps.title: Write the two-server plan
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: In your notes write DC01 = 10.50.0.10/24 and DC02 = 10.50.0.11/24. Use mask 255.255.255.0 and leave Default gateway blank on both. DC02 will use DC01 at 10.50.0.10 for DNS. Confirm the VMware host adapter does not already use .10 or .11.
steps.expected: Each server has its own address on 10.50.0.0/24. The public internet address is not in either server's adapter settings.

steps.lessonTitle: Build the isolated VMnet2 network
steps.title: Connect the guests to VMnet2
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: When each guest VM exists and is powered off, select it > VM > Settings > Network Adapter. Choose Custom: Specific virtual network > VMnet2 and enable Connect at power on. Keep one network adapter. Return here to check this after any temporary NAT update session.
steps.expected: Both guest adapters use the same VMnet2. After their static-address lessons, their live consoles show DC01 10.50.0.10/24 and DC02 10.50.0.11/24. The DC02 Windows lesson proves replies in both directions before promotion.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Choose Typical
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: In New Virtual Machine Wizard, select the radio button Typical (recommended). Click Next >. You should now see Guest Operating System Installation.
steps.expected: The wizard asks how the guest operating system will be installed.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Use manual Windows installation
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: On Guest Operating System Installation, select I will install the operating system later. Click Next >. You should now see Select a Guest Operating System. We attach the ISO later so Easy Install does not choose the Windows edition for you.
steps.expected: The wizard lets you choose a guest OS profile.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Choose the Server 2019 guest profile
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: On Select a Guest Operating System, click Microsoft Windows. Click the Version drop-down arrow. Select Windows Server 2019 from the list. Click Next > to reach Name the Virtual Machine. If that profile is absent, stop and check your Workstation version; do not guess a different OS.
steps.expected: The guest profile says Windows Server 2019.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Name the VM
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: On Name the Virtual Machine, click Virtual machine name, press Ctrl+A, and type DC01. Click Browse beside Location and select your dedicated lab folder on a drive with enough free space. Click OK in the folder chooser. Check the name and location, then click Next >. The next page is Specify Disk Capacity. This name labels the VMware library entry; it does not rename Windows.
steps.expected: The summary uses DC01 and a location you can find again.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Create a new virtual disk
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: On Specify Disk Capacity, click the Maximum disk size (GB) box. Press Ctrl+A and type 60. If Allocate all disk space now is visible, leave its checkbox clear. Select Split virtual disk into multiple files. Click Next >. The Ready to Create Virtual Machine page should now show the planned 60 GB disk; it is created only when you later click Finish. Splitting files controls how the disk is stored; leaving preallocation off lets it grow as data is written.
steps.expected: Ready to Create Virtual Machine shows the planned 60 GB disk. You have not clicked Finish yet.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Set memory and CPU
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: Click Customize Hardware. Select Memory and enter 2048 MB for a tiny practice DC. Select Processors: 1 processor, 1 core. If Windows updates or the desktop are too slow, shut down and raise memory to 4096 MB. These are practice allocations, not production sizing.
steps.expected: The Memory page shows 2048 MB (or your recorded 4096 MB fallback), and Processors shows one total core.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Attach the Server 2019 ISO
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: Select CD/DVD in the hardware list. Choose Use ISO image file, Browse to your Windows Server 2019 ISO, and enable Connect at power on.
steps.expected: The CD/DVD path ends with your Server 2019 ISO filename.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Attach the private VMnet
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: Select Network Adapter. Choose Custom: Specific virtual network and VMnet2 (Host-only) from LAB 03. Enable Connected and Connect at power on.
steps.expected: The VM is attached to the same private lab VMnet as the other lab servers.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Finish and start the VM
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: Click Close, then Finish. Select the new VM in the Workstation library and click Power on this virtual machine. Click inside its console and press a key when the ISO boot prompt appears.
steps.expected: Windows Setup appears inside the VM console.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Start Windows Setup

steps.expected: Setup displays an edition list or asks for a legitimate product key.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Choose Desktop Experience
steps.action: Select Windows Server 2019 Standard (Desktop Experience), or the matching authorized Datacenter (Desktop Experience) edition your course supplies. If using Evaluation for local practice, record that limitation. Click Next and accept the license only if you agree.
steps.expected: The selected line explicitly includes 2019 and Desktop Experience.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Install only on the new blank disk
steps.action: Choose Custom: Install Windows only (advanced). Select the new VM’s blank Drive 0 unallocated space and click Next. This is a clean install in a new VM, not the later Azure in-place upgrade.
steps.expected: Windows copies files, installs, and restarts.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Create the local Administrator password

steps.expected: The Windows sign-in screen appears.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Sign into the guest
steps.action: Use Workstation VM > Send Ctrl+Alt+Del (or Ctrl+Alt+Insert), then sign in as the guest’s local Administrator.
steps.expected: You see a Windows desktop and Server Manager.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Install VMware Tools
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro; then the named Windows guest
steps.action: In Workstation select VM > Install VMware Tools. In the guest open File Explorer > This PC, open the VMware Tools CD, and run setup64.exe if offered. Choose the normal setup and restart when asked.
steps.expected: After restart, the guest is usable with the expected mouse/display integration.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Patch the new Server 2019 guest
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro; then the named Windows guest
steps.action: This new guest is not domain-joined yet. Shut it down. In VMware choose VM > Settings > Network Adapter > NAT, keeping one adapter. Start Windows and set Ethernet IPv4 and DNS to Obtain automatically for this temporary update session. Open Start > Settings > Update & Security > Windows Update, check for updates and restart as required. Activate the evaluation while internet access is available. Shut down again, change the same adapter to Custom > VMnet2, and start the guest. The next network steps restore its planned static address and blank gateway before any domain work.
steps.expected: Windows has completed its pending restarts.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Rename Windows
steps.action: Inside the guest press Win+R, enter sysdm.cpl, and press Enter. On Computer Name choose Change. Enter DC01, confirm OK, and restart when prompted.
steps.expected: After signing in again, hostname returns DC01.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Open the guest IPv4 settings
steps.action: Inside the guest press Win+R, type ncpa.cpl, and press Enter. Right-click the connected Ethernet adapter > Properties. Select Internet Protocol Version 4 (TCP/IPv4), then Properties.
steps.expected: The IPv4 address and DNS fields are visible.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Enter the lab address
steps.action: For the example LAB 03 network only, choose Use the following IP address: 10.50.0.10; subnet mask 255.255.255.0; leave Default gateway blank (VMnet2 is host-only). Set preferred DNS to 10.50.0.10. Click OK and Close. If you changed the subnet in LAB 03, use your matching address plan instead.
steps.expected: ipconfig /all shows the planned 10.50.0.x address, blank default gateway, and the lab DNS address on VMnet2.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Confirm this is Server 2019
steps.action: Open Start, search Windows PowerShell, right-click it > Run as administrator. Run the read-only inventory below in this VM.
steps.command:
hostname
Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsProductName, WindowsVersion, OsBuildNumber
DISM /online /Get-CurrentEdition
steps.expected: WindowsProductName identifies Windows Server 2019; hostname identifies DC01.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Open Add Roles and Features
steps.action: Inside the named server open Server Manager. Choose Manage > Add Roles and Features. Click Next on Before you begin.
steps.expected: The Select installation type page is shown.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Select the local destination server
steps.action: Choose Role-based or feature-based installation > Next. Select a server from the server pool and select this VM’s computer name > Next.
steps.expected: The Server Roles page targets the correct computer.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Select AD DS and its tools
steps.action: Check Active Directory Domain Services. In the pop-up click Add Features, then Next.
steps.expected: AD DS is selected and its required management tools are included.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Install the role
steps.action: Keep the required Features selected. Click Next through the AD DS information page, review the selected target, then click Install.
steps.expected: Installation succeeds and offers Promote this server to a domain controller.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Choose the correct promotion operation
steps.action: Click Promote this server to a domain controller. Choose Add a new forest. Enter lab.example.test as Root domain name. Click Next.
steps.expected: The wizard shows a NEW forest named lab.example.test.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Set controller options and DSRM
steps.action: For Server 2019 in this lab, use Windows Server 2016 for both forest and domain functional levels. Keep DNS server and Global Catalog selected. Set and confirm a unique DSRM recovery password, store it securely, then Next.
steps.expected: Required options are selected and the password boxes have no validation error.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Review DNS and additional options
steps.action: Continue past the isolated-root DNS-delegation warning only if it is the expected warning for this private lab. Confirm the LAB NetBIOS name on Additional Options.
steps.expected: The wizard advances without a blocking validation error.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Keep the default AD paths
steps.action: On Paths keep the default NTDS database/log and SYSVOL locations for this small lab, then Next.
steps.expected: The wizard shows Review Options.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Check prerequisites before promotion
steps.action: On Review Options confirm lab.example.test, the correct computer, and DNS. Click Next, then wait for Prerequisites Check.
steps.expected: The prerequisite check succeeds; only understood lab warnings remain.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Promote and wait for restart
steps.action: Click Install only after the prerequisite check passes. Wait for the VM to restart; do not power it off to shorten the wait.
steps.expected: The guest restarts and offers a domain sign-in.

steps.lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Verify the directory
steps.action: Sign in with your authorized lab.example.test administrator account. Open Windows PowerShell as administrator in this VM and run the checks.
steps.command:
hostname
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object DNSRoot, NetBIOSName
Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.lab.example.test
steps.expected: The DNSRoot is lab.example.test and domain-controller records resolve to the lab’s private IPs.

steps.lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO

steps.lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO

steps.lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
steps.title: Open Group Policy Management
steps.action: In Server Manager choose Tools > Group Policy Management. Expand Forest: lab.example.test > Domains > lab.example.test.
steps.expected: The Operations OU appears in the policy tree.

steps.lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
steps.title: Create and link the GPO
steps.action: Right-click Operations > Create a GPO in this domain, and Link it here. Name it LAB-Operations-Banner and click OK.
steps.expected: The named GPO is linked under Operations.

steps.lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
steps.title: Edit the logon banner
steps.action: Right-click the linked GPO > Edit. Expand Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options. Set the interactive logon message title to LAB LAB and message text to This is a practice environment.

steps.lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
steps.title: Verify the objects
steps.action: On DC01 run these read-only checks and capture ADUC plus the GPO link.
steps.expected: The user, group membership, and GPO are returned.

steps.title: Start on your own Windows computer
steps.where: Your Windows computer at home · web browser

Use the Windows computer you will use to connect to the lab. Open your browser and go to https://portal.azure.com. Sign in with the Azure account used in the earlier lessons.
You will create the rule by clicking in the Azure website. PowerShell will only help you write down one value. You do not need Azure Cloud Shell, an administrator PowerShell window, or a connection to RHEL for this lesson.
An NSG, short for Network Security Group, is a list of network traffic rules. Inbound means coming into the Azure VM. Outbound means leaving it. Your connection leaves your Windows computer and arrives at the VM, so the VM needs an INBOUND rule.
SSH is the secure connection you will use to type commands on Linux from Windows. Port 22 is the numbered connection point SSH normally uses. This rule lets your home connection reach that point. You still need the correct username and SSH key to sign in.

On the left of the NSG page, click Inbound security rules. Click Add. In Source, select My IP address. Read the address Azure fills in. Write down the IPv4 address: four groups of numbers separated by dots. Do not click Add yet.
This public address is what Azure sees when your computer connects over the internet. It is usually the address of your home router’s internet connection. It is not the private address shown by ipconfig, and it is not the Azure VM’s address.
If you are using a VPN or browser proxy, the browser and SSH may use different public addresses. Use the approved network instructions to confirm the address SSH will use. Do not guess or turn off a required workplace VPN.

Run the first line below and press Enter. PowerShell asks you to type your public IPv4 followed by /32. Type the value you just wrote down and press Enter. Then run the second line.
$AdminSourceCidr is a named box in PowerShell memory. Read-Host asks you for text and puts your answer in that box. The second line displays it so you can check it. These lines do not create a rule or change Azure. If you close this tab, the value is forgotten; your written notes are the lasting record.

Set Source port ranges to *. Windows chooses a temporary outgoing port for each connection, so leave this field as *. This does not allow every source IP address; the address field above still restricts who can connect.

steps.title: Read the error before choosing a fix
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE, permissions are too open, or Load key: bad permissions means Windows SSH rejected the local private-key file. Use the key-permission steps below for that error.
Connection timed out means start with the VM power state, correct IP, inbound TCP 22 rule and network route. Connection refused usually means the destination was reached but no service accepted the port, or a device actively rejected it. Changing key permissions will not fix those problems.
Permission denied (publickey) by itself has several possible causes: wrong account, wrong key, missing authorized public key, server permissions or server policy. Check the actual VM build record. Do not guess another username or open SSH to everyone.
A host fingerprint prompt is a separate check. Compare it with the fingerprint obtained through the earlier Azure Run Command lesson before accepting. A changed or unfamiliar fingerprint is not permission to type yes automatically.

steps.lessonTitle: Create and inspect the rexuser key pair
steps.title: Find your Windows account, computer name and exact key file
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
Run whoami to see the signed-in Windows account. $env:COMPUTERNAME shows the computer’s name, not the processor model. Windows uses a SID, a stable account number, to identify the account even if its display name changes.
At the path prompt, enter the full path to the private key you already use. Do not include extra quote characters in the answer. The commands quote the variable for you, so spaces in a folder name are handled.
The private key may end in .pem or have no extension. Do not select its .pub partner. Never paste the key’s contents into the course or a support ticket.
steps.command:

# makes each example a shell comment. These placeholders demonstrate methods; they are not a request to install anything now.
chmod changes permission bits. u+x adds execute permission for the owner only. ./script.sh uses ./ to mean a file in the current directory, not one found through PATH. Review contents, source, integrity, and required interpreter before execution.
bash ./script.sh is an alternative that asks Bash to read the script; it normally needs read permission rather than an execute bit. It does not make a malicious script safe, and not every .sh file is meant for Bash.
sudo requests privileged execution. dnf install ./package.rpm installs a local RPM and resolves dependencies through configured repositories; ./ distinguishes the local file from a repository package name. Review package signature/source and the transaction before confirming.
tar handles archives. -t lists members, -x extracts, -z processes gzip compression, and -f says the next argument is the archive filename. Use listing before extraction and an empty staging directory; untrusted paths, links, or overwrite targets need review. Extraction alone does not install software.
Repository-based dnf install package-name selects a named package from enabled repositories. Trust the repository and package signatures, inspect the proposed transaction, and record the exact installed version.
steps.command:
# Reviewed shell script, two alternative invocation methods:
# chmod u+x ./script.sh
# ./script.sh
# OR: bash ./script.sh
# Reviewed local RPM:
# sudo dnf install ./package.rpm
# Inspect archive before extraction:
# tar -tzf archive.tar.gz
# tar -xzf archive.tar.gz
# Approved repository package:
# sudo dnf install package-name

steps.lessonTitle: Checkpoint: what is your rollback plan?
steps.title: Before anything changes: decide exactly what to back up
steps.where: Work administration workstation · change record and Veeam console (12 or 13)
steps.action:
Start with the VM you will change: select its whole-VM backup, including the OS disk and every data disk used by the application. For a new RHEL installation, back up the clean, working VM before installing Wazuh. After successful installation and verification, create a new accepted baseline; retain the pre-change recovery point according to policy.
If the change affects AD, DNS, domain membership or Group Policy, verify a recent application-aware backup of the domain controller first, including the volumes containing AD DS, SYSVOL and DNS-related state. Record domain-recovery access and the approved AD recovery procedure. A DNS export or GPO export alone cannot recover a domain controller. Do not casually revert a production domain controller snapshot.
For the Wazuh central host, include its OS, configuration, certificates, enrollment material and all disks containing indexer/event data. If manager, indexer and dashboard are separate VMs, identify all of them. A live disk copy is not automatically a consistent Wazuh/indexer backup: use the application recovery procedure or a coordinated clean shutdown in an approved outage. Do not independently restore mismatched cluster members.
For the RHEL endpoint or Windows client, include the OS, application data and agent configuration before agent installation, realm changes or hardening. Record its current manager association so recovery does not leave duplicate or stale enrollment. Back up only the affected systems and dependencies; an endpoint-only change does not require backing up every enterprise VM.
Save a protected change record outside the changed VM: hostnames, IP/DNS settings, disk inventory, package/kernel versions, service status, relevant configuration and rollback triggers. Keep credentials, private keys and recovery passwords in approved secret storage, never in the course GitHub repository. File hashes and screenshots are evidence, not backups.
steps.expected: A named list of affected VMs, all required disks, dependencies and application-consistency requirements exists before a backup job is selected.

steps.lessonTitle: Checkpoint: what is your rollback plan?
steps.title: Verify the backup scope and recovery access before taking a snapshot
steps.action:
Open Home → Jobs → Backup. Select the existing job → Edit. On Virtual Machines, confirm the exact VM is included; inspect exclusions and disk selection so required data disks are not omitted. Inspect Storage for the intended repository and retention. Use Cancel after read-only inspection; have the backup owner apply any required job changes.
For a Windows domain controller, inspect Guest Processing → application-aware processing and the per-VM application settings. Confirm guest credentials and processing success in the completed session, rather than merely seeing a checked option. Windows AD processing does not make an arbitrary Linux application consistent.
Check that the backup repository is outside the VM being changed, has capacity and remains reachable during recovery. Confirm the restore operator can access the backup and its encryption password independently of the affected machine/domain. Follow the workplace policy for an independent protected or immutable copy.
Ask the backup owner to verify the Veeam server configuration backup too. In the main menu select Configuration Backup and inspect its latest success, repository and encryption setting. This protects backup configuration; it does not replace VM backups. Store its encryption password separately in approved storage. Do not change enterprise backup settings as part of an endpoint lesson.
Run the approved VM backup using the later cards, verify the new per-VM restore point, and record a tested restore route. Only then take a short-lived vSphere snapshot immediately before the change if required. Backup first, temporary snapshot second, change third. This is a pre-change protection order, not a universal disaster-recovery restore order.
steps.expected: The current restore point covers the intended data, recovery access works, and application-specific restore limitations are recorded. Unknown coverage is a no-go.

Right-click the selected VM → Snapshots → Take Snapshot. Enter a unique name containing the change ID and time, and a description of the pre-change state.
For a planned cold checkpoint, shut down the guest cleanly first and confirm Powered off. Memory capture does not apply while powered off. For an approved powered-on checkpoint, decide whether memory capture is needed; it increases size/time. Filesystem quiescing requires working VMware Tools and is not automatically application-consistent backup.
Select Create/OK. Watch Recent Tasks until the snapshot task succeeds, then reopen Manage Snapshots to confirm its name/time. Record the evidence before starting the change.
Keep snapshots brief and remove them after validation and approval. Broadcom advises not retaining a single snapshot beyond 72 hours; workplace policy can require a shorter period. Snapshot deltas depend on base disks, so they are not standalone backups.

For an approved snapshot revert: right-click the exact VM → Snapshots → Manage Snapshots. Select the recorded pre-change checkpoint → Revert. Read the warning about losing later changes and confirm only within the approved outage/data-loss scope. Verify power state, guest access, storage and application behavior afterward.
For cleanup after a successful change: select the checkpoint → Delete. Deleting merges snapshot changes; it does not restore the earlier state. Monitor the task and datastore capacity. Do not select Delete All merely to remove one checkpoint.
If snapshots cannot meet the recovery requirement, use the enterprise backup restore plan. Test a recovery to an isolated destination when possible; never connect a duplicate restored identity to production by accident.

Get-VBRBackupSession lists history. It does not create a backup. Inspect the job session and per-VM task results in History; an old successful run is not proof of a current restore point.

steps.title: Choose one device or an approved subnet
steps.action:

A vSphere port group is not itself an IP subnet. Confirm the VLAN, subnet and routing used by the VMs attached to it. Allowing a subnet allows any device with a matching source address, not just VMs with a particular port-group name.
If the manager also runs in vSphere, there is no Azure NSG on that VM. Review RHEL firewalld and the actual network/NSX firewalls. If the manager is in Azure, also review its NSGs.
With private routed connectivity to Azure, use the private source range only if that range is actually preserved. With a public internet connection, Azure normally sees the company firewall’s translated public address. Use the confirmed public address or addresses, not an unreachable private range. One shared public address can represent devices outside the intended port group too.

hostname

This first rule is runtime-only and expires after ten minutes. Do not add a public-wide source. The checks below only confirm the rule was added; they do not prove other sources are blocked.

read -r -p "Approved source IPv4/32 OR subnet/CIDR: " SONIC_SOURCE

sudo firewall-cmd --zone="$SONIC_ZONE" --add-rich-rule="$SONIC_HTTPS_RULE" --timeout=10m
sudo firewall-cmd --zone="$SONIC_ZONE" --query-rich-rule="$SONIC_HTTPS_RULE"

The temporary runtime rule still expires, so schedule a controlled reload from the reviewed permanent configuration and retest. Keep recovery access; a reload also discards other runtime-only changes.

To remove this saved rule later, use sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone="$SONIC_ZONE" --remove-rich-rule="$SONIC_HTTPS_RULE", then follow the controlled reload and test procedure. steps.lessonTitle: Verify the endpoint RPM before installation
steps.title: Download and validate on Windows before transfer
steps.action:
Open Windows Terminal → PowerShell. Create a staging folder under your local profile. Paste the exact official RPM URL and the separate vendor SHA-512 value at the prompts. The digest must contain 128 hexadecimal characters; paste only the digest, not the filename.
Invoke-WebRequest downloads without executing the RPM. Get-FileHash calculates SHA-512 over the downloaded bytes. The comparison ignores hexadecimal letter case. Stop on an exception: check filename, release, architecture and algorithm, then download again from the official source. Never change the expected digest to make a failed check pass.
A vendor checksum checks against published bytes; it does not replace the signing-key and RPM signature checks below. Keep the digest in your change record.
steps.command:
$SonicStage = Join-Path $env:USERPROFILE "sonic-artifacts"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $SonicStage | Out-Null
$SonicRpm = Join-Path $SonicStage "wazuh-agent.rpm"
$SonicUrl = Read-Host "Exact official HTTPS RPM URL"
$SonicExpected = (Read-Host "Vendor SHA-512 digest only").Trim()
if ($SonicUrl -notmatch "^https://packages\.wazuh\.com/") { throw "Use the official package URL" }
if ($SonicExpected -notmatch "^[0-9a-fA-F]{128}$") { throw "Invalid SHA-512 value" }
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $SonicUrl -OutFile $SonicRpm
$SonicActual = (Get-FileHash -LiteralPath $SonicRpm -Algorithm SHA512).Hash
if ($SonicActual -ine $SonicExpected) { throw "CHECKSUM MISMATCH: do not transfer or install" }
Write-Output "VENDOR SHA-512 MATCH"
$SonicActual
steps.expected: VENDOR SHA-512 MATCH appears before you transfer anything.

steps.title: Make a practice folder
steps.action: Create a practice folder under your home and move into it. mkdir -p creates missing parent directories. Use Tab to complete names and the Up arrow to recall a command.
steps.expected: pwd ends with DesktopPractice and the folder is inside your home.

steps.lessonTitle: Learn the Commands You Use Every Day
steps.title: Create, copy and rename
steps.action: Write two lines to a practice text file. > replaces that named file; do not aim it at valuable files. Copy first, then rename the copy.
steps.command:
cd ~/DesktopPractice
printf "first line\nsecond line\n" > notes.txt
cp -i notes.txt copy.txt
mv -i copy.txt renamed.txt
cat renamed.txt
steps.expected: You have notes.txt and renamed.txt with the same two lines.

steps.lessonTitle: Learn the Commands You Use Every Day
steps.title: Search and inspect
steps.action: Find files and filter text. A pipe sends one command’s output into the next. Use less to page through longer output and press q to leave.
steps.command:
cd ~/DesktopPractice
grep -n "second" notes.txt
wc -l notes.txt
find . -maxdepth 1 -type f
ls -lah | less
steps.expected: grep returns the matching line and wc counts two lines.

steps.lessonTitle: Learn the Commands You Use Every Day
steps.title: Learn help and interruption
steps.action: Use --help or man for syntax; q exits man. Ctrl+C interrupts a foreground task; Ctrl+Shift+C copies selected text in GNOME Terminal. Never paste a command you cannot explain.
steps.expected: You can find an option’s meaning and exit a pager.

steps.lessonTitle: Learn the Commands You Use Every Day
steps.title: Clean only your practice copy
steps.action: Use interactive removal for the renamed practice copy. Confirm only after checking its full path, then verify the original remains. Avoid rm -rf as a routine cleanup habit.
steps.expected: notes.txt remains and the chosen practice copy is gone.

steps.lessonTitle: Manage Files and Permissions
steps.title: Navigate with Files
steps.action: Open Files from Activities. Open Home, Documents and Downloads. Ctrl+L enters a path; type ~/DesktopPractice and Enter. Ctrl+H toggles hidden files.
steps.expected: You can locate the same practice file from GUI and Terminal.

steps.lessonTitle: Manage Files and Permissions
steps.title: Create and organize
steps.action: In Files create an Everyday folder in Documents. Copy notes.txt into it, rename the copy, and open it with the text editor. Use Trash for unwanted practice copies.
steps.expected: Your copied document opens and the original is still present.

steps.lessonTitle: Manage Files and Permissions
steps.title: Understand permissions
steps.action: Check a file you own. Apply mode 600 to the practice notes only: owner read/write, no access for group/others. This is not full-disk encryption.
steps.expected: ls shows owner-only read/write on that practice file.

steps.lessonTitle: Manage Files and Permissions
steps.title: Create an archive
steps.action: Use Files → right-click the Everyday folder → Compress (menu labels can vary). Choose a ZIP filename. Extract it into a temporary folder and open the copied note.
steps.expected: The extracted note matches your original.

steps.lessonTitle: Manage Files and Permissions
steps.title: Use removable storage
steps.action: Connect a USB data drive and open its entry in Files. Copy a harmless sample, wait for transfer completion, then use Eject/Unmount before disconnecting.
steps.expected: The sample reopens and the drive disconnects without a busy warning.

steps.lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
steps.title: Inspect your existing software sources
steps.action: DNF manages system RPMs and dependencies. GNOME Software may show RPM and Flatpak sources. List enabled DNF repositories and check package details before installing.
steps.command:
dnf repolist
dnf info firefox
dnf search libreoffice
steps.expected: You know which repositories are currently enabled.

steps.lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
steps.title: Install a native everyday app
steps.action: For an office suite use the AlmaLinux repository package libreoffice if available. Read the package source, extra packages the app needs and download size, then approve the install. Start it from Activities.
steps.expected: A document opens in the installed app.

steps.lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
steps.title: Install Flatpak support
steps.action: Install the Flatpak client from your configured AlmaLinux repositories. Then check existing user remotes. System and user remotes are different scopes.
steps.command:
sudo dnf install flatpak
flatpak --version
flatpak remotes --user
steps.expected: flatpak is available and your user remote list is visible.

steps.lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
steps.title: Add Flathub only after reviewing the source
steps.where: AlmaLinux VM · web browser for Flathub; then GNOME Terminal
steps.action: Open the official Flathub AlmaLinux setup page linked below. If you accept this third-party source, add it to your user only. Check its URL afterward.
steps.expected: The user-scoped flathub remote points to the official source.

steps.lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
steps.title: Install an app and review permissions
steps.action: Search for VLC, check the exact Flathub app ID and source, then install the user-scoped example only if you accept its publisher and permissions. Launch from Activities or Terminal.
steps.command:
flatpak search VLC
flatpak remote-info --user flathub org.videolan.VLC
flatpak install --user flathub org.videolan.VLC
flatpak info --user --show-permissions org.videolan.VLC
flatpak run org.videolan.VLC
steps.expected: VLC starts and opens a non-sensitive local media sample.

steps.lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
steps.title: Update and remove deliberately
steps.action: Update RPMs with DNF and user Flatpaks separately. Before removing an app, review extra packages the app needs and preserve needed data. Flatpak uninstall without --delete-data normally leaves user app data.
steps.command:
sudo dnf upgrade --refresh
flatpak update --user
flatpak list --user --app
steps.expected: You can explain the two update paths and identify an app’s source.

steps.lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
steps.title: Check hardware and game support first
steps.where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
steps.action: Read the game’s official Linux/Steam requirements. Check GPU support and the current Steam/Proton information. Anti-cheat, DRM and Windows-only launchers may prevent play; some games require Windows.
steps.expected: You selected one compatible test title and recorded the hardware expectation.

steps.lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
steps.title: Inspect and install Steam from Flathub
steps.action: Check the exact Steam application ID on Flathub and its permissions. The Flatpak wrapper is community maintained. Review requirements and accept the install only if it fits your system.
steps.command:
flatpak remote-info --user flathub com.valvesoftware.Steam
flatpak install --user flathub com.valvesoftware.Steam
flatpak info --user --show-permissions com.valvesoftware.Steam
steps.expected: Steam is installed in your user Flatpak scope.

steps.lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
steps.title: Start and sign in
steps.action: Launch Steam from Activities or Terminal and let its client updates finish. Sign in privately; never capture the password, QR code or Steam Guard code for evidence.
steps.expected: You reach your own Steam Library.

steps.lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
steps.title: Try a native title first
steps.action: Choose a small Linux-native title that meets the VM or physical machine’s graphics capability. Pick the default library location, check required space, and download it. Launch and record the actual result.
steps.expected: The supported test game launches, or you record the specific compatibility failure.

steps.lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
steps.title: Test Proton separately
steps.action: In Steam → Settings → Compatibility check Steam Play/Proton options. For a compatible Windows title, use its Properties → Compatibility to choose an offered supported Proton version when needed. Test one title at a time.
steps.expected: You can distinguish native Linux execution from a Windows game using Proton.

steps.lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
steps.title: Keep libraries and runtimes healthy
steps.action: Update user Flatpaks and Steam. Use Steam Settings → Storage to view library usage. For an external library first complete the WD storage class and grant only that path to the Steam sandbox.
steps.expected: You know where the game is stored and how much free space remains.

steps.lessonTitle: Configure Network, Printing and Sharing
steps.title: Inspect network before changing it
steps.action: Use Settings → Network or Wi-Fi for your connection. A VMware VM usually sees virtual Ethernet even when Windows uses Wi-Fi. Check active connections and addresses.
steps.command:
nmcli connection show --active
ip -br address
ip route
steps.expected: You identify the right adapter and active connection.

steps.lessonTitle: Configure Network, Printing and Sharing
steps.title: Separate DNS from connectivity
steps.action: Resolve a known official site, then test HTTPS. If name lookup fails but your network route exists, check the connection’s DNS details before changing anything.
steps.command:
getent hosts almalinux.org
curl -I https://almalinux.org
nmcli device show
steps.expected: You can tell a name-resolution error from an HTTPS or connection error.

steps.lessonTitle: Configure Network, Printing and Sharing
steps.title: Add a printer
steps.action: Open Settings → Printers, unlock if requested, choose Add, and select an allowed detected printer or its confirmed IPP address. Print a single test page.
steps.expected: The queue exists and the actual test page prints.

steps.lessonTitle: Configure Network, Printing and Sharing
steps.title: Configure peripherals
steps.action: In Settings → Bluetooth pair one device if supported. Test input/output under Sound. In a VM pass through a specific USB device only when needed, then disconnect it when finished.
steps.expected: The chosen device works, or its unsupported state is documented.

steps.lessonTitle: Configure Network, Printing and Sharing
steps.title: Access a known file share
steps.action: In Files → Other Locations enter the approved smb://server/share address. Use an account authorized for that share and test with a harmless file. Disconnect afterward.
steps.expected: The authorized share opens without changing server permissions.

steps.lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
steps.title: Identify how the drive reaches AlmaLinux
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: On a physical AlmaLinux PC connect the intended USB drive, or power off and follow the PC manual for an internal SATA installation. In VMware, USB passthrough can attach an external disk exclusively to the guest. For learning, prefer adding a separate NEW virtual disk while powered off. Never use raw access to your Windows system disk.
steps.expected: The drive appears in AlmaLinux without formatting or partition changes.

steps.lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
steps.title: Match model, serial and capacity
steps.action: Open Activities → Disks. Select the candidate drive and record its model, serial, size and partitions. Compare with the physical device label. Check terminal output too; do not assume /dev/sdb is always the WD drive.
steps.expected: You positively distinguish the data drive from the system disk mounted at /.

steps.lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
steps.title: Use an existing data volume without erasing it
steps.action: If it contains files, select its existing partition in Disks and use Mount (play button), or open it from Files. Do NOT choose Format Disk, Format Partition or Delete. Record the actual mount path from Disks and check your own files.
steps.expected: Existing files are visible and unchanged.

steps.lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
steps.title: Prove copy access and available space
steps.action: For a writable mounted volume copy only your harmless notes.txt using Files, reopen it, and compare its SHA-256 with the source. In Terminal quote the ACTUAL mounted path when using df -h or findmnt -T. Do not run a placeholder as a path.
steps.expected: The sample file matches and free space is shown for that mounted filesystem.

steps.lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
steps.title: Optional: prepare a NEW empty practice disk
steps.action: Skip this step for any drive containing data. On a separate practice blank virtual disk, reconfirm identity in Disks, use its menu → Format Disk → GPT if a partition table is needed, then the + button → Create Partition → choose ext4 for Linux-only practice and a label such as PracticeData. Formatting ERASES selected content; review the device and deletion prompts before confirming.
steps.expected: Only the explicitly empty practice disk has the new Linux filesystem.

steps.lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
steps.title: Choose persistent mounting only if needed
steps.action: Existing removable drives can simply mount from Files when plugged in. For a dedicated Linux data disk, in Disks select the partition → gear → Edit Mount Options; record the existing options, use stable UUID identification, a deliberate path such as /mnt/WDData, and nofail for an optional disk. Test while attached before a reboot. Do not edit the root mount.
steps.expected: The chosen data volume mounts at its intended path and the machine still boots.

steps.lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
steps.title: Understand what space you added
steps.action: A disk mounted at /mnt/WDData increases storage available at that path; it does not enlarge /. Keep files there intentionally. On a new empty ext4 practice mount only, use Files as an administrator or a reviewed one-directory ownership change for your user; never recursively chown an existing data tree.
steps.expected: You can explain which filesystem gains files and which remains unchanged.

steps.lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
steps.title: Use it for games or disconnect it safely
steps.action: For Steam use a Linux-native dedicated library folder on this mounted drive. Grant only that ACTUAL folder to the user Steam Flatpak (via a permissions manager or reviewed flatpak override --user --filesystem=EXACT_PATH com.valvesoftware.Steam), then add the library in Steam Settings → Storage. When done close apps and unmount/eject before unplugging.
steps.expected: The correct library path is visible, or the data volume ejects cleanly.

steps.lessonTitle: Back Up Your Desktop and Restore a File
steps.title: Choose what matters
steps.where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
steps.action: List Documents, Pictures, project files, browser exports and game saves you need. Include needed hidden app data deliberately. Do not assume an installed app is the same as its documents.
steps.expected: You have a short backup scope and destination.

steps.lessonTitle: Back Up Your Desktop and Restore a File
steps.title: Make a dated sample backup
steps.action: In Files create a dated backup folder on your verified external destination. Copy the Everyday folder and practice notes. Wait for completion, then safely unmount the destination.
steps.expected: The copied files exist on a different device.

steps.lessonTitle: Back Up Your Desktop and Restore a File
steps.title: Prove restore without overwriting
steps.action: Reconnect the destination and copy the sample into ~/RestoreTest using Files. Open it and compare hashes for the original and restored file.
steps.command:
sha256sum ~/DesktopPractice/notes.txt
# Also hash your actual restored file path; compare the full values.
steps.expected: Restored content matches and opens.

steps.lessonTitle: Back Up Your Desktop and Restore a File
steps.title: Schedule a repeatable habit
steps.where: AlmaLinux VM · backup notes and calendar
steps.action: For this first class, use the manual Files backup you just tested. Set a weekly reminder in your calendar to copy the chosen folders into a new dated folder on your backup drive. Keep earlier copies until you check the new one. Write down when you last restored a sample, where the backup lives and who can unlock any encryption. You can choose an automated backup tool later; do not call a scheduled copy a tested backup until you have restored from it.
steps.expected: Your plan says when to back up and how to recover.

steps.lessonTitle: Back Up Your Desktop and Restore a File
steps.title: Keep VM snapshots separate
steps.where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
steps.action: Use powered-off VM snapshots for short experiment rollback, and separate backups for valuable data. Review snapshot growth and remove obsolete snapshots using Workstation’s supported manager.
steps.expected: You can explain rollback versus independent file recovery.

steps.lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
steps.title: State the problem precisely
steps.action: Record what failed, when, the app, the last change, and whether it happens to all users or one. Reproduce using a harmless action and capture the exact error.
steps.expected: You have one testable problem statement.

steps.lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
steps.title: Check resources
steps.action: Check space, memory and running processes. In top press q to exit. A full filesystem can break updates and app state.
steps.expected: You can identify the filesystem or process actually consuming resources.

steps.lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
steps.title: Inspect services and recent errors
steps.action: Read failed units and the current boot’s warning/error journal. Journal access can require authorized sudo; check before changing a service.
steps.expected: You can relate an error timestamp and service to the symptom.

steps.lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
steps.title: Inspect one service deliberately
steps.action: For an actual named failed service, use systemctl status SERVICE and journalctl -u SERVICE -b. Replace SERVICE with the real unit from your previous check. Research the specific error before a restart.
steps.expected: You know the failing dependency/configuration or what saved result is missing.

steps.lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
steps.title: Respect SELinux and firewall boundaries
steps.action: Check SELinux state and active firewall policy. If an app is denied, check its logs and the official supported labeling/port guidance. Do not disable SELinux or firewalld as the default workaround.
steps.expected: You recorded current protection state without weakening it.

steps.lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
steps.title: Recover and prove the fix
steps.action: Reverse only the identified change, restore an app config backup, or use the VM recovery checkpoint if necessary. Repeat the original test and save before/after evidence.
steps.expected: The original problem is resolved or narrowed with clear next evidence.

steps.lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
steps.title: Understand where commands execute
steps.where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
steps.action: The hosted website is copy/help mode. GNOME Terminal runs Bash inside your AlmaLinux VM. The local SONIC companion starts PowerShell on Windows; its WSL tab is a separately installed WSL distro, NOT your VMware VM.
steps.expected: You can name the machine each shell controls.

steps.lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
steps.title: Install Node.js and Git, then start the local app
steps.action: On your Windows host, open Start, type Windows PowerShell and open it. Follow the linked terminal setup guide to install Node.js LTS (which includes npm) and Git with its PowerShell commands. Close and reopen PowerShell or use the guide’s PATH refresh command. Run node --version, npm.cmd --version and git --version before continuing. In File Explorer, open the downloaded academy project folder, click its address bar, type powershell and press Enter: that opens PowerShell in the correct project folder. Run the block below there; npm.cmd avoids a blocked npm.ps1 script without weakening your execution policy.
steps.command:
Set-Location $env:USERPROFILE
git clone --branch main https://github.com/CloudSeamTech/SONIC-Academy.git
Set-Location .\SONIC-Academy
npm.cmd ci
npm.cmd run dev
steps.expected: SONIC opens on localhost, normally port 3000.

steps.lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
steps.title: Start the companion in a second Windows window
steps.action: From the same repository root in a second PowerShell window install the packages the companion needs and start it. Keep this process open. The random pairing token is private and stays on your computer.
steps.command:
npm.cmd run companion:install
npm.cmd run companion:start
steps.expected: The companion prints a loopback address and pairing token.

steps.lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
steps.title: Connect and prove a real Windows result
steps.where: Your Windows host · web browser at http://localhost:3000/migration#view=terminal
steps.action: At http://localhost:3000/migration#view=terminal select Windows PowerShell. Paste the token into the local-only field and Connect locally. Run Get-Date twice. Compare with your own Windows clock.
steps.expected: Live date/time output appears from your current Windows account.

steps.lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
steps.title: Optionally enable SSH inside the AlmaLinux guest
steps.action: For VMware access use GNOME Terminal to install/start the SSH server and check its address and firewall. If SSH is not already allowed, add the ssh service only to the active connection’s firewall zone after checking it. This opens private-network SSH access; NAT needs no public port-forward. In firewall-config select the active zone and check the ssh service only for that private connection, then make the reviewed change permanent if needed. Alternatively use firewall-cmd --zone=<your-active-zone> --add-service=ssh, replacing the placeholder; repeat with --permanent only after testing.
steps.command:
sudo dnf install openssh-server
sudo systemctl enable --now sshd
ip -br address
sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all
steps.expected: sshd is active and you know the guest’s actual NAT address.

steps.lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
steps.title: Verify host identity and connect from Windows
steps.where: AlmaLinux VM · Terminal; then Windows host · PowerShell
steps.action: In the guest check the ED25519 host-key fingerprint. In Windows PowerShell use ssh your-user@the-actual-guest-IP and compare the offered fingerprint before accepting. The text user/IP are placeholders; substitute your own. Use native PowerShell for a full interactive SSH session; the SONIC panel can relay basic prompts but is not a full-screen terminal emulator.
steps.command:
sudo ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub
# Above: AlmaLinux guest only. Then run ssh with your actual user/IP in Windows.
# After SSH connects: whoami; hostname; cat /etc/os-release
steps.expected: You reach the intended AlmaLinux host and can verify its release and username.

steps.lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
steps.title: Use the right terminal and shut down cleanly
steps.where: AlmaLinux VM · GNOME Terminal; then local academy browser on your Windows host
steps.action: Run AlmaLinux desktop commands in GNOME Terminal or your verified SSH session. Use exit to leave SSH. In SONIC choose Disconnect and stop the companion process with Ctrl+C when finished. Stop the local dev server separately.
steps.expected: Remote/local prompts are distinguishable and the companion is no longer listening when stopped.
